variants.name: CompletableFuture completion stages
variants.implementation_notes: java.util.concurrent.Future is only the read end - get() blocks, isDone() tests, cancel() is best effort - while CompletableFuture adds the write end: complete, completeExceptionally or cancel makes it ready and exactly one of them succeeds, and CompletionStage composition (thenApply, thenCompose, thenCombine, allOf, anyOf) replaces blocking waits. Java has no await syntax, so method chains are the idiom; pass an explicit Executor to async stages, because without one they run on ForkJoinPool.commonPool, and consider virtual threads when the code must keep blocking.
pitfalls: get() blocks and wraps the real failure in ExecutionException (unwrap with getCause()) while join() throws CompletionException - and a CompletableFuture nobody joins hides its exception until someone does.
Async stages without an explicit Executor run on ForkJoinPool.commonPool, so a blocking call inside one steals shared threads; supply the executor and use virtual threads for blocking code.

variants.name: ExecutorService + blocking Future.get (classic)
variants.implementation_notes: The classic form the pattern arrived with on the JVM: the executor is the scheduler, submit returns a Future, and the consumer waits when it needs the value - optionally with a timeout and with cancel(true) as a best-effort cancellation that only interrupts interruptible calls. Use it for simple fan-out where the caller must wait anyway or the surrounding code is synchronous; move to CompletableFuture when consumers should be notified instead of blocked, and to virtual threads when many tasks must block.
pitfalls: get() without a timeout turns a stuck task into a stuck caller, and cancel(true) only helps where the task actually checks interrupts - a tight loop keeps running.
One platform thread per pending task is the scalability cliff: thousands of outstanding operations mean thousands of parked threads, which is the problem virtual threads were introduced to remove.

variants.name: Virtual-thread-per-task executor
variants.implementation_notes: JEP 444 makes one thread per pending task affordable again: each task runs on its own virtual thread, a blocking wait unmounts the virtual thread instead of pinning its carrier, and the caller collects an ordinary Future with an ordinary blocking get(). The handle stays exactly as before, but the runtime reason to avoid blocking disappears, which is why the platform positions plain blocking code plus structured scopes as an alternative to reactive composition in high-throughput services.
pitfalls: Virtual threads remove the cost of blocking, not the need to bound work: unbounded fan-out through a virtual-thread executor still floods downstream resources.

Blocking inside synchronized blocks or native frames pins the carrier thread, and the carrier pool is finite - prefer ReentrantLock for long blocking sections and keep thread-affine caches out of the design.
